record.title: BabelArena tests agent execution across 23 languages and reports resource-linked failure gaps
record.summary: A September 20 preprint introduces BabelFlow, a workflow for adapting agent benchmarks across languages while preserving links among prompts, tools, environments and evaluators, and releases BabelArena with 16,146 instances across 23 languages. In a 40-task Chinese ablation, the authors report fewer broken references and behavioral mismatches than independent translation, at higher token cost. Their five-model evaluation reports lower task success and language consistency in the low-resource language group, with distinct tool-use/control-flow failures and increased input-token use in sampled tasks. These are paper-reported findings; translation validity, independent reproduction and generalization remain open.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v1 paper describes BabelArena as 16,146 instances built from 702 canonical tasks across four benchmark families, 13 domains and 23 languages, with all benchmark components adapted to preserve executable task structure.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a 40-task Chinese adaptation ablation, the authors report that BabelFlow reduced broken references from 20.0% with independent translation to 2.5%, and observed behavioral mismatches from 5.0% to 0%; the workflow used 3.35 times the baseline translation-token cost.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five tested models, the paper reports lower average task success and language consistency for its low-resource language group than for its high-resource group. In sampled VitaBench failures, Thai and Tamil had larger shares of tool-use and control-flow errors than English and Chinese; low-resource VitaBench trajectories used 1.69–2.06 times as many input tokens on matched tasks with similar turn counts.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that its translated benchmarks preserve every source task’s cultural or semantic validity, nor that the measured language gaps generalize to other models, tasks or deployment populations; no independent evaluation was inspected.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent team reproduced the BabelFlow construction comparison or the five-model BabelArena evaluation.

Quality assurance uses a 200-text sample per language; high-resource translations receive expert scoring, while medium- and low-resource translations are scored by GPT-5.6-Sol. Equivalence and cultural validity outside the sampled tasks remain unknown.
The five-model results and error breakdowns cover four adapted benchmarks and selected samples; broad model, task and deployment coverage is not established.

brief.importance_rationale: If the benchmark construction and evaluation findings generalize, multilingual agent reliability must be measured across tools, environment text and control flow rather than translated prompts alone; the reported token overhead also has direct operating-cost implications. The current evidence is one preprint’s four benchmark families and five model runs, with limited independent language-quality auditing.
limitations: Single author-team preprint; no independent reproduction inspected.
The translation workflow’s 40-task ablation is conducted only for Chinese; it uses 3.35 times the independent-translation token cost.
Language quality is sampled at 200 strings per language; GPT-5.6-Sol, rather than human language experts, scores medium- and low-resource samples.
Five models and four source benchmark families do not establish broad deployment performance; some failure analyses use selected trajectory samples.
brief.summary: A September 20 preprint introduces BabelFlow, a workflow for adapting agent benchmarks across languages while preserving links among prompts, tools, environments and evaluators, and releases BabelArena with 16,146 instances across 23 languages. In a 40-task Chinese ablation, the authors report fewer broken references and behavioral mismatches than independent translation, at higher token cost. Their five-model evaluation reports lower task success and language consistency in the low-resource language group, with distinct tool-use/control-flow failures and increased input-token use in sampled tasks. These are paper-reported findings; translation validity, independent reproduction and generalization remain open.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report fewer benchmark adaptation defects with BabelFlow and language-dependent agent performance/cost differences. For matched VitaBench tasks, low-resource trajectories reportedly use 1.69–2.06× the input tokens of English trajectories with similar numbers of turns; no wall-clock or monetary cost was measured in that comparison.
technical.compute_or_cost: The 40-task Chinese workflow ablation uses 3.35× the baseline translation-token cost; measured inference cost impact is not reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint specifies a 16,146-instance benchmark, four source benchmark families, 13 domains and 23 languages, plus its adaptation and evaluation protocol. This review inspected the paper but did not execute benchmark code or independently assess translations.
technical.mechanism: A coding agent traces runtime data dependencies to identify text fields and execution-critical values; translation types separate preserved identifiers/assets from free prose and canonical entity translations. Multiple agents check structure, cross-artifact consistency, semantic fidelity and behavioral equivalence; human reviewers adjudicate defects before acceptance.
technical.regime: The paper evaluates five named frontier models at medium reasoning effort across four benchmark families and 23 languages. A construction ablation adapts 40 tasks into Chinese. Translation quality samples 200 texts per language; language-failure analyses include selected benchmark trajectories.
technical.reproducibility: The paper is publicly accessible on arXiv. This activation did not execute the benchmark or validate released task artifacts.
technical.strongest_baseline: For construction defects, BabelFlow is compared with independent field translation and canonical translation on the same 40 source tasks; model evaluation retains each source benchmark’s scoring procedure but is not a matched comparison against a single-language control for every language/model.

brief.title: BabelArena tests agent execution across 23 languages and reports resource-linked failure gaps
brief.why_it_matters: Translating only user prompts can leave tools, databases, parsers and scoring rules inconsistent, so multilingual agent tests need to cover executable workflows. BabelArena’s paper reports that lower-resource language runs show differences in task success, tool/control-flow failures and input-token use. These findings can change evaluation design and inference-cost estimates, but they remain single-team results on selected benchmarks and languages.
